description: macOS may check for updates AND install them. The check runs in Rust, so unlike a webview fetch it is not subject to CORS -- which is why the macOS customer was once never told a new version existed at all: the manifest URL redirects to release-assets.githubusercontent.com, which sends no Access-Control-Allow-Origin, so the browser rejected the response before the app saw it and the catch resolved to null. INSTALL WAS WITHHELD UNTIL 2026-09-01 on the stated grounds that 'a minisign-only artifact cannot replace the stable OS-signed bundle and change its code requirement'. MEASURED against the shipped app, that premise is false: codesign reports Signature=adhoc, flags=(adhoc,linker-signed), TeamIdentifier=not set, and spctl rejects it with 'no usable signature'. There is no OS-signed bundle and no code requirement to protect, so the guard cost every Mac customer a manual download to defend a property this build does not have -- the owner reported exactly that symptom: auto-update opens the GitHub releases page instead of updating, and their install sat two releases behind. What DOES protect the artifact is minisign: the updater verifies the .app.tar.gz against the pubkey compiled into the binary before replacing anything, so an attacker without the private key cannot ship an update. That is real tamper protection and it is independent of Apple. RE-EVALUATE WHEN DEVELOPER ID SIGNING LANDS: once the bundle is genuinely signed, CI must sign the .app.tar.gz too, or an unsigned update really would break the code requirement this description used to invoke.
